claims.text: Introducing a high density of twin boundaries can enhance ductility in MnNiSi-based magnetic-refrigeration materials.
Introducing a high density of twin boundaries can enhance toughness in MnNiSi-based magnetic-refrigeration materials.
Twin-boundary engineering can largely retain the high magnetocaloric effect of MnNiSi-based materials.
Controlled thermomechanical processing can induce a high density of twin boundaries in MnNiSi-based materials.
The intervention is designed to leave the overall chemical composition unchanged.
Near-room-temperature annealing and deformation can promote twin formation in the target material.
Calibrated annealing and deformation parameters can avoid significant residual stress and microstructural phase changes while producing twins.
Twin boundaries act as barriers to crack propagation.
Twin boundaries facilitate more uniform plastic deformation.
Barrier action against cracking and more uniform plastic deformation improve toughness and ductility.
Leaving composition unchanged will leave the intrinsic magnetic ordering responsible for the magnetocaloric effect largely unaltered.
The processed material will show more than a 10% improvement in mechanical performance relative to conventionally processed material.
The processed material will retain magnetocaloric entropy change within approximately 5–10% of the unprocessed baseline.
Unwanted phase changes or excessive internal stresses could affect magnetic interactions and compromise magnetocaloric performance.
The expected benefit is conditional on preserving the magnetic phase responsible for the magnetocaloric effect.
The quantitative magnetocaloric response may vary with processing parameters.
Failure to improve mechanical performance by more than 10%, or a reduction of magnetocaloric entropy change by more than 10%, would falsify the hypothesis.
